uncited: Surface shading effects apply local illumination models to volumetric data to create the appearance of solid surfaces, shadows, and ambient occlusion within participating media.
This family solves the problem of volumes appearing as featureless fog by introducing directional lighting, self-shadowing, and indirect light approximation.

It differs from sibling methods like [Lighting Models](2056-lighting-models.md) by focusing specifically on surface-like appearance cues (normals, shadows) rather than general scattering phase functions, and from [Two-Pass Shadow Casting](2196-two-pass-shadow-casting-kajiya-and-von-herzen.md) by typically evaluating shading per-sample during ray marching rather than via separate geometry passes.
The concept of applying surface shading to volumes originated with the need to give volumetric clouds and fog a tangible, solid appearance rather than looking like flat fog.
